sent.t: The other time I told him about the nine things he should never put in his mother's coffin.
Today it's his turn to open the other box, the one they take home.
In 1998, here in Analco, three blocks from my funeral home, a lady opened her father's urn three days later.
She spoke to me crying.
Not because he was missing his father, because there was a plastic bag inside, a metal plate with a number and a gray powder that seemed
to her like another person and she was right to doubt.
I have been in this for more than 40 years.
I buried more than 6,000 people between Guadalajara and San Antonio, Texas.
All that time I saw what comes out of the oven hundreds of times.
Today I am going to tell you exactly what is in that urn, how much it weighs, what should not be there, and the four questions
that I would ask before signing.
In the end I will tell you what I would do with the urn of my own mother.
But first, the first, because here begins a deception of the word.

When you say ashes, you imagine a fine powder, like the ash of a cigarette, like the ash of coal.
It is not that.
What comes out of the oven are bones, fragments of bone, white, gray, the size of a nail, of a beans, some bigger.
In the trade we say remains.
In the United States they call it cremence, which is an invented word, half cremate, half remence, burnt and remains, because there they didn't dare to
say ashes.

In almost all cremation packages that are sold in Guadalajara, the urn that is included is a temporary urn.
Temporal means, of thick cardboard, or MDF, or cheap resin, with a plastic lining inside.
It is made to take the remains from the funeral home and to last as long as a funeral.

Profeco raises funeral service prices and recommends exactly this, ask for the quote by writing, row by row and compare between funerals before signing.
In the United States it is easier, because the federal law, the funeral rule of the FTC, forces the funeral home to give you the general
price list, with each service and each article separately, and forbids you to charge for a urn that you bought elsewhere.
In Mexico there is no such law.
That is why here the paper has to be asked by you.
And there is a detail that almost no one asks, and that to me seems the most important of all.
The urn that they give you, can you bury it?
Because there are urns of resin and pressed cardboard that cannot stand the earth.
And there are pantheons that do not allow you to bury a loose urn, nor in the family grave, without a concrete box or without a
niche.
Chapter 6 The Bellorio without body.
Before going to where the urn goes, I want to talk about something that is charged and that almost nobody understands, the velorio.
In Mexico there are two ways to hire a cremation, the first is called direct cremation, the body leaves the hospital or the house, goes to
the velorio and from there to the crematorium, no hay sala, no hay café, no hay capilla.
La familia se reúne en su casa o en la iglesia y a los dos o tres días recibe la urna.
La segunda se llama velación y cremación.
Usted paga la sala de velación, las horas, el ataúd, el personal, el café, las sillas, el servicio religioso si lo quiere.
El cuerpo se vela, se reza, se abraza y después va al horno.
La diferencia de precio no es poca.
En Guadalajara, una cremación directa anda entre 8 mil y 14 mil pesos.
Una velación de 24 horas con cremación puede andar entre 18 mil y 35 mil.
Y en el medio hay todo, doce horas, ocho horas, sala chica, sala grande, capilla con aire, capilla sin aire.

Paga el tiempo, paga el cuarto, paga que la familia tenga un lugar donde llorar junta.

In the Mezquitán, in the one in Guadalajara, in the municipal pantheons, there are niches in the walls and there are columbariums.
The price depends on the pantheon, on the height, whether it is new or used, and whether it is for a lifetime or for years.
A niche in a municipal pantheon can cost from a few thousand pesos to more than 20,000, depending on the place, and you have to add
the refrain if it is temporary.
If you want to bury the urn in a grave, in the tomb of the family, you have to ask the pantheon, not the funerary.
Many pantheons allow burying the urn in the same grave, above or next, if the grave has space and if the family has the title.
Others ask for a concrete box, others do not allow it and if you bury the urn without warning the day they open the grave for

most done in Mexico and the one that is least said loud the urn stays in the house in the room on the altar next to
the photo with its fan and that's fine, that's a family decision and it's as respectable as a niche.
But if he stays at home, there are two things he has to know.
One, the urn has to be sealed and in a dry place.
Two, the day the family moves or the house is sold or the lady who took care of it dies, someone has to know where that
paper is and who it belongs to.
I have seen urns being left in houses that were sold and I have seen families fighting for an urn in a trial.
I don't want anyone to do it.
Chapter 8.
The papers that nobody asks for.
There are three papers in a cremation, three, and almost nobody asks for them complete.
The first is the act of defunction of the civil registry.
That is known to everyone.
The second is the cremation permit.
It is signed by the health authority or the civil registry, according to the state, and without that permit the crematorium cannot open the oven.
If the funeral home tells you that the permission is taken later, it is not true, it is taken before.
The third is the one that almost nobody asks for, the act or constancy of cremation.
It is a role of the funeral home or the crematorium with the date, the time, the name of the crematorium, the name of the one
who entered and the number of the plate.
That role is the one that allows you to then move the urn to another state or another country or put it in a niche or
show anything in 2012 a family from San Antonio looked for me for a very specific reason they had come to Jalisco with the urn of
the grandmother on the plane in the handbag and in the pantheon here they asked for the paper of the cremation, they did not have it,
the funeral there had been given, but it had been lost in the move, it took five weeks to get it, with calls and with a
notary, and the grandmother was five weeks in a box in the room of a cousin, waiting, and if the body cremated in the United States,
and the remains come to Mexico, there is one more role, the permit for transit of remains, that some states ask and others do not, and
that the airline will ask if the urn is documented.
Ask it.
It costs less to ask it than to get it later.

Chapter 10.
The funeral that already charged him.
There is a topic that in Mexico is huge and of which almost nobody speaks with clarity.
The funeral that already charged him.
The plan of provision.
El famoso ya tiene todo pagado.
Doña Cuca lo tiene desde 2009.
Pagó en abonos, con una libreta, y le dieron un contrato y una carpeta.
Me lo enseñó el mes pasado, y le hice tres preguntas, las mismas que le haría cualquiera.
Primera, ¿dónde está el dinero?
It is not the same for the funeral home to keep their money in their safe, to keep it in a fideicomiso, or in an insurance
company, or in a plan that is registered.
If the funeral home breaks, or changes owner, or closes, who responds?
In Mexico there are funeral plan provisions that are pure private contract.
If the company disappears, you have a paper, and a paper does not bury anyone.
Second, is the price frozen or adjusted?
This is the most important question and one that almost nobody does.
Almost all the forecast plans in Mexico do not freeze the price, they freeze the service.
You paid the service from 2009 to the price of 2009, but the day it is used, you are charged the difference between today's price and
what you paid.
